analysis.one_liner: Imposes federal licensing, background checks, waiting periods, an assault weapons ban, and gun industry liability changes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in December 2022 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every gun buyer and owner to obtain a federal license with safety training and repeated background checks, extend background checks to all private sales, impose a seven-business-day waiting period, ban semiautomatic assault weapons and silencers, raise the buying age to 21, let courts remove guns from people deemed dangerous, allow gun makers to be sued, and fund community violence intervention and research. It was introduced on the final days of the 117th Congress and died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by gun violence: potential victims of mass shootings, domestic violence survivors, families at risk of suicide and accidental shootings, and communities served by violence intervention programs. It also gives judges, police, and courts tools to remove firearms from people judged dangerous.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a federal license to purchase or possess firearms and ammunition, with safety training, background checks, and renewal every 10 years.
Extends background checks to most private firearm transfers and imposes a minimum seven-business-day waiting period for purchases.
Bans the manufacture, sale, and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices.
Creates a federal extreme risk protection order process letting family members or police ask a court to remove guns from someone judged a danger.
Expands domestic violence protections to include dating partners and people convicted of misdemeanor stalking.
Removes civil liability limits on gun manufacturers so victims can sue, and lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission set safety standards for guns, locks, and safes.

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners face new licensing, training, and registration requirements and a longer wait to buy. Gun and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers face higher excise taxes, stricter dealer security and record-keeping rules, liability exposure to lawsuits, and a ban on a category of products they sell. Law-abiding 18-to-20-year-olds lose the ability to buy firearms or ammunition.

drawbacks.text: The licensing requirement means otherwise law-abiding citizens could face criminal penalties for possessing a firearm without a license, with penalties up to 2 years in prison.
Raising the minimum age to 21 restricts firearm purchases for adults 18 to 20, though it provides exceptions for employment, farming and ranching, target practice, and military service.
Dealers, manufacturers, and importers face higher excise taxes on firearms and ammunition.
Extending the Gun-Free School Zones Act to colleges and universities could affect students and staff on campus who are licensed to carry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims to reduce gun violence through licensing, waiting periods, and removal tools, with real benefits for victims and communities. The costs fall heavily on gun owners and industry, and the licensing regime raises civil-liberty concerns for otherwise lawful owners, given criminal penalties for unlicensed possession. It is a broad package whose design reflects a strongly regulatory approach.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with two days left in the session and referred to three House committees, it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on December 20, 2022, with Congress adjourning January 3, 2023.
Referred to the House Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce committees.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and dealers face no new licensing, tax, or liability requirements, and gun owners avoid new licensing duties; communities waiting on violence intervention funding did not benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun industry and existing gun owners

for.name: 10 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Carson, Moulton, Norton, Trone, Maloney, Lynch, Pressley, McGovern, Auchincloss, and Keating.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsors. No vote or hearing occurred, so no opposition actions appear in the record.

industries.note: The bill bans a product category (assault weapons and large-capacity magazines), raises excise taxes on guns and ammunition, repeals the 2005 law shielding manufacturers from civil liability, and allows CPSC safety standards, all of which reduce or add costs to the industry's sales and legal exposure. Its loss of liability protection was the industry's main protection from litigation.

Dealers must certify security plans to deter theft, submit to new record-keeping and inspection requirements, report lost and stolen inventory, and conduct background checks on employees, adding compliance costs.
Owners face mandatory licensing, training, storage, and registration requirements, while sporting-goods and gun retailers could see fewer customers from the higher minimum age and waiting periods.

industries.industry: Gun violence prevention organizations and community violence intervention providers
industries.note: The bill authorizes federal grants for community violence intervention programs and for research on gun violence prevention, expanding funding for these groups.
